summary: Describes using the Unix Compress algorithm to compress PPP packets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The well-known Unix squishing program is applied to the data on a PPP link.

questions: how does unix compress work with ppp
how does synchronization work in ppp compression
subtitle: The LZW compression algorithm applied to Point-to-Point Protocol links.

tldr.problem: PPP links are often slow, and transmitting data over slow links is costly. Compression can reduce the amount of data transmitted, but only if it is efficient enough and synchronized reliably.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies the use of the Unix compress algorithm (LZW - Lempel-Ziv-Welch compression) for PPP packet compression. It includes negotiation of compression parameters, a packet format with sequence numbers, and automatic compression ratio checking to turn compression off when it stops being effective.
tldr.outcome: PPP implementations can optionally use BSD compression to reduce bandwidth usage on slow links. The algorithm was widely available as free software and saw extensive use on modems and early network links.

today: RFC 1977 is an Informational RFC describing a compression method from 1996. Although dial-up modems and PPP are no longer common, the fundamental principles of adaptive dictionary-based compression remain relevant. Modern compression algorithms like DEFLATE (used in gzip and PNG) build on similar concepts. The RFC demonstrated that compression negotiation and synchronization are critical to reliable data transmission.

sections.title: Compression for Point-to-Point Links
sections.content:
PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) is used on slow links such as dial-up modems. On such links, bandwidth is scarce and expensive. Compression can significantly reduce the amount of data transmitted, improving throughput and reducing cost.

The RFC specifies how to use the Unix Compress algorithm (based on LZW compression) to compress PPP packets. This algorithm was chosen because it was freely available, widely implemented, and had proven effective over many years of use for compressing network news (Usenet) transmitted over slow modem links. The algorithm is dynamic, adapting as it learns about the data being transmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Slow internet connections are expensive. A well-known squishing method can send the same data with fewer bytes, speeding up transfers and saving money.

sections.title: How LZW Compression Works
sections.content:
LZW (Lempel-Ziv-Welch) compression builds a dictionary as it processes data. Initially, the dictionary contains single bytes (0-255). As the algorithm encounters sequences it has seen before, it adds new entries to the dictionary. When it sees a sequence that matches a dictionary entry, it outputs the dictionary code instead of the literal bytes.

For example, if the data contains the byte sequence "ABC" multiple times, the compressor adds an entry "ABC = code 512" to the dictionary. The next time it sees "ABC", it outputs code 512 instead of three bytes, saving space.

The compressor periodically checks the compression ratio. If the ratio becomes too high (data is not compressing well), it clears the dictionary and starts over. This prevents the dictionary from filling with entries that are not helping. The compressor also automatically turns off compression for individual packets that would expand if compressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm learns which groups of bytes appear often, and replaces them with shorter codes. If the learning is not working, it forgets everything and starts fresh.

sections.title: Packet Format and Negotiation
sections.content:
Before BSD compression can be used, both sides of the PPP link must negotiate it using the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP). The negotiation specifies the code size (how many bits long each compressed code can be), which ranges from 9 to 16 bits. A common choice is 12 bits, allowing up to 4096 dictionary entries.

Each compressed BSD packet contains a 2-byte PPP protocol field (value 0xFD or 0xFB), a 2-byte sequence number, and the compressed data. The sequence number starts at zero when the dictionary is cleared and increments after each packet, including uncompressed packets. This allows the receiver to detect missing or out-of-order packets.

Not all packets are compressed. Packets with PPP protocol numbers in the range 0x0000 to 0x3FFF (except 0xFD and 0xFB) are never compressed; instead they are sent in their original form but processed through the compression dictionary for learning purposes. This ensures both sides keep their dictionaries synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: Two sides agree on how big the dictionary can be. Each compressed packet is numbered so they can tell if any got lost. Some packets are never squished but still help train the dictionary.

sections.title: Synchronization and Reliability
sections.content:
LZW compression requires that both the compressor and decompressor maintain identical dictionaries. If a packet is lost or arrives out of order, the dictionaries become out of sync, and decompression fails. The RFC handles this with sequence numbers: if the receiver detects an unexpected sequence number, it knows a packet was lost and requests dictionary resynchronization.

When resynchronization is needed, the receiver sends a CCP Reset-Request to the sender. Both sides then clear their dictionaries and resume compression. The sequence numbers are reset to zero. The receiver must discard all compressed packets until it receives a Reset-Ack, to ensure both sides truly start fresh.

Packet loss on a busy link often triggers multiple out-of-order errors before the Reset-Ack arrives. To handle this, the receiver may send additional Reset-Requests, but it should not send them more frequently than the round-trip time of the link to avoid unnecessary dictionary clears.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must know the same dictionary or it does not work. If a packet gets lost, they stop, agree to forget their old dictionary, and start fresh.

sections.title: Performance and Adaptation
sections.content:
The memory requirements for BSD compression are modest. A code size of 12 bits (a common choice) requires less than 64 KB of memory on both sender and receiver. Code sizes of 9 to 15 bits are practical.

The algorithm automatically adapts to the type of data being transmitted. Text (like email or web pages) typically compresses very well because it contains many repeated characters and words. Binary data (like executables or images) often does not compress well and may even expand. The algorithm detects this and stops compressing packets that would expand, sending them uncompressed instead.

When compression becomes less effective (the compression ratio falls), the algorithm clears the dictionary and starts learning again. This prevents the dictionary from filling with entries that have become irrelevant. The algorithm also increases the code width dynamically: it starts with 9-bit codes and expands to wider codes as it fills the dictionary, squeezing the most value from available dictionary space.
sections.plainLanguage: Text squishes great. Pictures do not. The algorithm notices and stops trying when it does not help. It forgets old patterns when they are no longer useful and learns to use bigger codes when needed.

sections.title: Software Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC includes the C source code for the compression and decompression functions, derived from the 4.3BSD Unix compress command. This code is portable to any system with a C compiler and uses only standard data types (16-bit shorts and 32-bit ints).

The algorithm performs well on RISC processors with many registers. However, the included code is specific to Unix systems with mbufs (memory buffers); implementors on other systems may need to adapt it. The BSD copyright notice on the code allows free use for any purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The code comes with the RFC and is free to use. It works on standard computers but might need adjustment for different operating systems.
